tier_reason: First-party README chart (image with an embedded ns table) states .NET 7 and a Ryzen 9 5950X, and the benchmark code is public (sandbox/Benchmark/Benchmarks/SerializeTest.cs, DeserializeTest.cs). No build config, flags or BenchmarkDotNet job settings are given, and the struct-array gain is over 50x, so the tier is capped at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: "For standard objects, MemoryPack is x10 faster and x2 ~ x5 faster than other binary serializers. For struct array ... up to x50 ~ x200". The chart's own ns table shows narrower gains against the named baselines. JsonResponseModel (47 fields, nested): MemoryPack 13,176/24,540 ns ser/deser vs MessagePack-CSharp 22,961/39,420 (1.74x / 1.61x), protobuf-net 73,028/51,640 (5.54x / 2.10x), Orleans 58,530/46,210 (4.44x / 1.88x) and JsonSerializer 189,099/308,900 (14.4x / 12.6x). Vector3[10000]: MemoryPack 231/316 ns vs MessagePack-CSharp 9,887/26,335 (42.8x / 83.3x) and protobuf-net 53,769/39,526 (232.8x / 125.1x). All ratios are derived from page data.
corrections.caveats: The README chart image does carry a numeric ns table (serialize and deserialize for JsonResponseModel and Vector3[10000]). Against MessagePack-CSharp the standard-object gain is only ~1.6-1.7x, so the README's 'x2~x5' holds only for protobuf-net and Orleans, and 'x10' is against System.Text.Json. The struct-array win is a blittable memcpy-style path. The chart dates from 2022 on .NET 7 with MessagePack-CSharp 2.4.x. The checked-in benchmark project now targets net8.0 with MessagePack 2.4.35, so it is not v3 and not exactly the setup that made the chart. Build config and flags are not stated; hardware is Ryzen 9 5950X.

notes: The entry is real and the baseline comparison is genuine. The downgrade is for the overstated standard-object multiplier against MessagePack-CSharp: the page's own table gives ~1.6-1.7x, not 2-5x. Tier stays C. Metadata checked: MIT, 4,739 stars, last commit 2026-07-08, not archived and not a fork.

tier_reason: First-party benchmark with public code (benchmarks/bench_encodings.py, run with -p msgpack). It states CPython 3.11 but gives only '~2020 x86 Linux laptop' as hardware, with no CPU model and no C compiler or flags, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page text: msgspec is "measurably faster than other Python MessagePack libraries like msgpack or ormsgpack". Per-iteration times are embedded in the page source as results_msgpack and plotted in ms. msgpack 1.0.7: encode 0.403 ms, decode 0.799 ms. msgspec with no schema: 0.125 / 0.487 ms, so 3.23x encode, 1.64x decode and 1.96x round-trip. msgspec structs: 0.112 / 0.348 ms, so 3.62x encode, 2.30x decode and 2.62x round-trip. All ratios are derived from page data. The '5x to 60x' figure on the same page is only for Struct order comparison against attrs/dataclasses/pydantic and does not apply to MessagePack.
corrections.workload: MessagePack encode/decode of a generated filesystem-like tree of 1000 File/Directory objects (make_filesystem_data, timeit autorange), msgspec 0.18.5 vs msgpack 1.0.7 and ormsgpack 1.4.1 on CPython 3.11
corrections.caveats: The MessagePack numbers are not SVG-only. The page embeds the raw per-iteration timings in JS (Vega plot), and ratios come from those. The win over msgpack is ~2-2.6x round-trip, mostly on encode (3.2-3.6x), with decode 1.6-2.3x. The results date from msgspec 0.18.5. Hardware is vague ('~2020 x86 Linux laptop', no CPU model) and the C compiler and flags are not stated.

notes: The comparison against msgpack-python is real and numeric. The downgrade is because claimed_speedup attached an unrelated '5-60x' (Struct order-comparison) figure; the real MessagePack gain is ~2-2.6x round-trip. Tier stays C. The last commit on main is 2026-09-24 (pushed_at is 2026-09-25, probably another branch). Checked: BSD-3-Clause, 4,128 stars, not archived and not a fork.
